newsitem.title: SPAIN: INSTANT VIEW -Spanish CPI rises to 1.6 pct in June.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -Spanish CPI rises to 1.6 pct in June.

text.p: Following is a selection of economists' reactions to Spain's Consumer Price Index, which rose 1.6 percent year-on-year in June, as expected, after 1.5 percent in May. Core inflation was 1.9 percent June, unchanged from 1.9 percent in May.
VALENTIN FERNANDEZ, ECONOMIST AT CREDIT LYONNAIS, MADRID

"This data is exactly in line with market expectations. Both numbers, the general index and the core are both exactly as expected. So it is going to be neutral for inflation, which hit a low in May and has actually been picking up since, but at a moderate pace.

This data also doesn't change anything for monetary policy - we expect an official rate cut at the end of September, not before. Economic growth is strong and the Bank of Spain does not need to stimulate it. By September the Bank of Spain will have some news about the 1998 public budget, and will also have more information about the inflationary trend. By then it is also likely we will know something more about the mechanism to fix currency parity versus the euro. This CPI number will not have a big effect on the market, it has been already discounted."
COLIN WARREN, ECONOMIST AT TOKAI BANK, LONDON

"It's not a bad number. Services inflation (up 0.3 percent vs May, 3.2 percent year-on-year) is not particularly brilliant. People will now start to look for demand side pressures in areas not exposed to competition...The Bank of Spain's target next year is going to be difficult if services inflation proves stubborn. With consumer demand roaring away, what's important for Spain is that price expectations start to go down."
FRANCESCO GIORDANO, ECONOMIST AT CSFB IN LONDON

"To me this data is a bit disappointing. Core inflation climbing 0.2 percent in the month is a little bit too much. Food (down 0.4 in the month) is giving a good contribution to keeping inflation down, but this almost hides that service inflation (up 0.3 in the month and 3.2 percent in the year) is stubbornly high. My forecast for the end of the year remains unchanged at 2.0 percent y/y and remains similar to our forecasts on German inflation. So this new June data adds nothing, but if anything, it is a bit worriesome.

"I have seen a few analysts suggesting September as the appropriate time for another monetary easing. To me this is a bit too early. I would say by the end of the fall. The only problem the Bank of Spain could face is that the peseta could be pushed higher. They are buying -- currency reserves rose two percent in May and June.
So later in the year, with a further public budget tightening of the order of 0.5 percent of the gross domestic product, maybe they will have the room to compensate with another cut."
FERNANDO GUTIERREZ, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT ARGENTARIA, MADRID

"It was a good number. Prices for services are stuck at (year-on-year) rates around three percent. The situation in services hasn't changed, it remains the same. It is the most worrying component, although CPI below two percent isn't alarming.
"We believe the Bank of Spain isn't going to cut interest rates before summer. It will wait for the budget."
ANTONIO MIGUELANEZ, ECONOMIST AT BBV, MADRID

"It doesn't seem like a bad number. The service prices exceeded our forecasts (0.2 percent). But this is only a relative worry considering that the overall number is in a downward mode. The outlook is favourable. We don't see any significant deviation in the most volatile components including food which could fall more.
"We believe the Bank of Spain is going to maintain interest rates until after summer, probably until they present the budget for 1998.
